opus-5.5.text:
For me, that desire was probably the single biggest factor. Toward the end of my PhD I was weighing industry research labs against academia, and both had real appeal. Industry offers enormous resources, compute, engineering support, and in robotics, access to hardware and data at a scale that's hard to match at a university. I took that seriously.

What kept pulling me back was the question: who decides what problem I spend the next five or ten years on? In industry, even in very good research labs, your agenda eventually has to connect to the company's priorities. That's not a bad thing, but priorities shift, and sometimes the problem you care most about isn't the one the organization needs solved this quarter.

As a faculty member, the freedom is almost uncomfortable at first. Nobody tells you what to work on. You have to build your own taste and conviction about what matters. In robotics, I think some of the most important problems, like how robots can learn general skills from diverse data or reason over long-horizon tasks, need sustained, patient investment, and you don't always know if it'll pay off. Academia lets you make those longer bets.

There's also the freedom to choose who you work with. Picking students, shaping how they think and grow as researchers, is a big part of the job, and I find it really meaningful. Your impact isn't just your papers. It's the people who go on to do their own work.

Of course, that freedom comes with trade-offs: fundraising, teaching, service, and much more responsibility for keeping the lab running. But for me, the ability to define my own research direction and follow my curiosity outweighed all of that. Once I framed the decision around autonomy, the faculty path felt like the natural choice.

r001.rationale: The response compares industry research labs with academia and describes faculty autonomy, but it does not present starting a company as an alternative route.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, that desire was the core of it. When I was finishing my PhD, I thought hard about going into industry, and the pull was real: more compute, more engineering support, a much faster path to seeing your work in a product. But every time I pictured it, I kept coming back to the same question, which was who gets to decide what problem I work on next.

In a company, even a great research lab, the roadmap ultimately belongs to someone else. That is fair, because they are paying the bills. But I have always been happiest when I could follow a question just because it bothered me, even if it didn't obviously connect to anything anyone was shipping. A lot of my work in robot learning came from that kind of stubborn curiosity, like asking why a robot that can imitate a demonstration still falls apart on a slightly longer task, and then chasing that for years.

Academia is the one place where that is not just tolerated, it is the job. You write the grant, you pick the direction, you recruit students who are excited about the same thing, and if it turns out to be a dead end, that is on you. I actually find that accountability motivating. The tradeoff is that you give up resources and speed, and you have to be comfortable being a little behind the biggest labs on scale. I decided that was worth it, because the thing I wanted most was to own the questions, not just the answers.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts working in industry with pursuing academia as a way to choose research questions, but it does not mention starting or founding a company as an alternative route.

astra-6.text: The ability to choose what I work on was a big part of why I wanted to pursue a faculty position. I wanted the freedom to follow questions that I find interesting and important, even if they don’t have an immediate payoff. Of course, being a faculty member comes with constraints and responsibilities, so it’s not complete freedom. But the opportunity to set a research direction and build a team around it was really appealing to me.

sol-6.1.text: I think the biggest draw was the freedom to decide what I wanted to work on. A faculty position seemed like an opportunity to develop my own research agenda—to choose the questions I thought were important and pursue them over a longer period of time. Of course, that freedom comes with responsibility: you have to find resources and support your students. But the possibility of building a group around those questions was a big part of what attracted me to that path.
